paragraphs: I am a Full Stack Software Engineer delivering scalable enterprise solutions across fintech, banking and tax compliance for clients including USAA and Vertex Inc. I bring end-to-end SDLC expertise in Java, Spring Boot, Angular, microservices, AWS and Azure, combined with hands-on experience developing AI agents and integrating multiple LLMs.

I use Claude, Specification-Driven Development (SDD) and Research, Plan, and Implement (RPI) methodologies to accelerate delivery. I have contributed to DevOps, Center of Excellence (CoE) and Vertex Agent Platform (VAPOR) initiatives spanning engineering improvements, enterprise metrics and application delivery, with recognition for innovation, internal platform development and multiple hackathon wins.

bullets: Designed and developed AI-powered engineering agents, including PR Fix and Fail-to-Fix agents, integrating multiple LLMs to automate development workflows, code analysis and issue resolution; collaborated with the VAPOR (Vertex Agent Platform) team to build cluster-based AI agents for end users.

Built TechScout, an end-to-end application using React.js and Node.js, contributing to frontend development, backend services, API integration and delivery; also enhanced the Connected Tax Platform (CTP) with application features, chat-based interfaces and AI-agent capabilities.

Contributed to Center of Excellence (CoE) initiatives by developing reusable skills, commands and AI agents that standardized workflows and improved developer productivity; collaborated across AI engineering, DevOps, CoE and platform development teams on organization-wide solutions and engineering practices.

Contributed to the Vertex Unified Metrics Platform to support centralized, consistent engineering measurement, while supporting DevOps and deployment workflows, including n8n deployments and automation that streamlined delivery and operations.

Applied Specification-Driven Development (SDD) and Research, Plan, and Implement (RPI) methodologies with Claude to structure requirements, plan implementations and accelerate AI-assisted software delivery.

Developed an in-house quiz application as an alternative to third-party solutions, earning organizational recognition and prize money. Also achieved multiple hackathon wins through innovative application development and AI-driven solutions.

Developed and maintained enterprise engineering applications using Core Java, Spring Boot, Spring Cloud, Spring Data JPA, RESTful Web Services and microservices across banking, insurance and enterprise-security projects for USAA and Citi Bank.

Contributed to USAA's Classic to Talon Migration (C2T) by analyzing legacy integrations, designing as-is and to-be API flows and developing migration strategies; designed, documented and published REST APIs using OpenAPI and Swagger 2.0 to improve discoverability and developer onboarding.

Integrated downstream APIs for secure microservice communication, optimized SQL queries and database operations, and implemented unit tests using JUnit and Mockito, achieving 85%+ test coverage and helping reduce production defects.

Deployed and monitored applications on OpenShift, analyzed pod logs through the OpenShift Web UI, and used Kibana and Elasticsearch to investigate application behavior, traffic patterns, active server instances and production issues.

Contributed to Citi Bank's Service Account Migration (SAM) by migrating service accounts to CyberArk, implementing secure integrations with Core Java and Spring Boot, and decommissioning deprecated accounts to strengthen credential security and reduce attack surface.

journal.title: PR Fix Agent: a code reviewer that is always available
paragraphs: In many teams a pull request waits for a human reviewer before it can move forward. The PR Fix Agent gives the developer feedback first. When a pull request is opened or updated, it reviews the changes, looks for bugs, security problems and quality issues, and posts its findings on the pull request.
It does more than point out problems. It suggests specific fixes with examples and explains why each change is recommended, so developers learn while they fix.

The benefits are easy to see. Developers get feedback before human review, teams get consistent reviews across everyone's code, and managers get a steady way to improve code quality and catch security issues earlier.

Building it meant combining large language models with the pull request workflow and designing instructions (prompts) that give clear, useful and safe feedback. Like any product, it keeps improving through user feedback and usage data.

journal.title: Fail-to-Fix: from a failed build to a suggested fix
paragraphs: When an automated test run fails, a developer usually has to open long reports and logs to work out what broke. Fail-to-Fix does that first step automatically.

It reads the failed test results, finds which tests failed and why, and asks an AI model to suggest fixes. Earlier fix attempts are included as context, so suggestions for similar failures can build on what worked before.
The suggestions are posted on the pull request as a clear review comment, with inline code suggestions where possible, so the fix starts where the developer is already working.
It runs as a reusable step in the team's build pipeline, so any project can switch it on without building its own.

journal.title: VAPOR: one safe place to build AI agents
paragraphs: An AI agent is more than a language model. It is the model plus planning, memory, tools and safety rules around it. Building all of that for every new agent takes a lot of time, and it is easy to get wrong.

VAPOR is the internal platform that provides this once, for everyone. Teams describe the agent they want, connect their own data, and the platform supplies the runtime, a catalog of approved models and tools, and monitoring of every run.

It also checks agents before release. A readiness check looks at simple questions, such as whether the tools are limited to what the agent needs and whether risky actions need a human to approve them. The same setup always gives the same result, so there is no guesswork.
I work with the platform team to build agents on it. The main lesson is that good AI products need trust and clear rules as much as clever models.

journal.title: TechScout: making technology requests simple
paragraphs: When a team wants to start using a new tool or technology, it usually needs a review first, to check that it is safe, useful and allowed. Doing this with scattered tickets and emails makes it hard to see where a request is, and who is waiting for whom.

TechScout puts the whole process in one web application. A person submits a request, the right reviewers pick it up, the technology is evaluated, and a decision is recorded. Every request has a clear status, and each step has rules about who can move it forward.

I built it end to end: the screens people use, the backend services behind them, the connections between the two, and the pipeline that delivers new versions. Later work focused on improving the existing features, making pages load faster and gathering user feedback.
What I learned: a workflow looks simple on the screen, but the rules behind each status change are where most of the care is needed.

journal.title: Connected Tax Platform: one place for tax work
paragraphs: Tax software is often split into many separate products, and users have to jump between them to finish one job. The Connected Tax Platform changes this by organising the experience around the work people actually do, from start to finish.
A good experience here starts with structure. Before every feature is ready, the team decides how things are grouped, named and found, so that a new user can see where to go next without training.
My part was building features on this platform, including chat-based interfaces and AI-agent capabilities, so users can ask for help or get answers next to the task they are doing.
The lesson for me: good products are shaped around the user's journey, not around the internal product boundaries.

journal.title: Unified Metrics: one set of numbers for everyone
paragraphs: When every team measures its work in its own way, it is hard to compare results or trust a report. One team's "daily users" or "test status" may mean something different from another's.

The Unified Metrics Platform fixes this with shared definitions. Products send their measurements in a common format, the platform combines them, and dashboards show the results. Typical topics are product usage, how fast changes reach customers, how well tests are passing, and how healthy services are.
A good design goal is to make it easy for a team to join. Common measurements can be collected automatically, so teams do not have to write extra code before they see useful numbers.
I contributed to the platform, and I supported DevOps and deployment automation around it. What stays with me is that a metric is only useful when people agree on what it means.
